A new study with data from mice and human tissues suggests that, in ulcerative colitis, immune cells in the gut might make pain-sensing nerves hypersensitive.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

People with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) experience gut pain that can be severe, and it doesn't always go away when their inflammation is under control and their colonoscopy looks normal. Now, in a new laboratory study, researchers found a previously unknown pain pathway that may explain this phenomenon.

The findings, published Oct. 23 in the journal Science Immunology, also point to a potential way to block that pain.

"Inflammation in the gut has always been thought of like a fire: the sensory nerves alarm because of the smoke and the heat, and when the fire is put out the alarm should stop," said study co-author Dr. Heng Xu, a physician at Ninth People's Hospital in Shanghai. Xu and his colleagues set out to try to isolate what could be causing the pain even when there's no visible "fire" or "smoke."

"What we found is that the tissue itself changes consistency," Xu told Live Science in an email. "It becomes stiff and less elastic, a bit like a scar, and that stiffness alone keeps triggering the alarm even after the fire is out."

In ulcerative colitis, the most common form of IBD, inflammation causes ulcers in the gut, as well as symptoms like bloody diarrhea and abdominal cramping. Several medications can help quell this inflammation, but that doesn't necessarily eliminate patients' pain. The researchers wondered if immune cells that live in the gut might contribute to that ongoing pain.

They zoomed in on a protein called Piezo1; in immune cells, it's known to play a role in inflammation, and in neurons, it contributes to pain signals. The team looked at whether this protein's activity changed in the context of colitis.

"We started with sequencing data that reads cells one at a time, from the gut tissue of patients with ulcerative colitis and from mice with the disease," Xu said. "One cell type stood out: an immune cell that lives permanently in the gut wall, rather than arriving from the bloodstream when there's trouble." The quantity of these cells was higher in colitis than in healthy guts, and the cells carried more Piezo1 than the other cells analyzed.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"They sit touching the nerve endings," Xu added.

In several experiments with lab mice with colitis, the team used a probe to press on the gut tissue and measure how hard it was. This showed that, compared with healthy mice, the gut was stiffer in two models of disease: one with visible inflammation and another with almost none.

They also measured pain levels in both sets of mice. "In mice with almost no visible gut inflammation, the pain was still there, which is why a colonoscopy can look normal while the patient hurts," Xu said.

They then looked at Piezo1 in both sets of mice. The protein sits in the immune-cell membrane, and when the stiffened tissue around it is pulled or squeezed, it's as if a button were pressed and a channel opens, Xu said. This sets off a chain reaction that leads to pain, Xu said.

That's because calcium ions rush into the cell via the channel, and that surge sends a protein called NF-kB from the cell's interior fluid into its nucleus — the control center where DNA is stored. There, NF-kB plugs into a gene, ordering the cell to manufacture nerve growth factor (NGF) that then exits the immune cell.

This NGF, which is known to amplify pain signals in the body, interacts with nearby pain-sensing neurons. These nerve endings grow denser and become hypersensitive, which makes ordinary gut activity painful, the study suggests.

This newly described mechanism could help explain why ulcerative colitis patients can sometimes contend with pain even when their colonoscopies look normal.

The researchers used chemicals as on-off switches for Piezo1 in immune cells, opening the channel with one and closing it with another. As they did this, they tracked calcium signals and NGF production, and both rose and fell in step with the switch. This result suggests that Piezo1 activity is both necessary for this response and, on its own, enough to trigger it in these cells, Xu said.

Blocking this chain of events abolished the pain hypersensitivity in both sets of mice. The researchers tried completely removing the Piezo1 gene from the gut immune cells and found that this eliminated the pain. Removing the gene also caused no problems in healthy mice, they noted.

The study was "well controlled," said Hongzhen Hu, the scientific director for the Mark Lebwohl Center for Neuroinflammation and Sensation at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, who was not involved in the research. Future research should address the chemical messengers that coordinate inflammation, called cytokines, and determine whether the same chain reaction occurs in human cells, he said in an email.

The mouse experiments also may not reflect long-term, chronic disease in patients, given the mice experienced symptoms only transiently, Xu said.

Xu and his colleagues are now aiming to develop a drug that can target Piezo1 to switch off gut pain locally without suppressing the entire immune system. This would be a more targeted treatment than current options, such as immunosuppressants or opioids.

Other scientists have explored using anti-NGF treatments for other chronic pain conditions but not for ulcerative colitis, Xu noted. Fully blocking NGF might have downsides, he said, since NGF also helps to maintain nerves.

So more work is needed to translate these findings into a treatment. But for now, the work sheds new light on how immune cells can detect a physical change — such as tissue becoming stiff — and convert it to a pain signal.

"For the pain field, that's a conceptual shift," Xu said.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Wu, L., Shen, T., Wang, Z., Wang, T., Hu, X., Sun, M., Zhang, L., Cheng, Y., Hao, Y., Zhou, L., Lin, M., Bian, J., Feng, J., & Xu, H. (2026). An autonomous macrophage-nociceptor mechanosensory relay drives chronic visceral pain. Science Immunology, 11(124). https://doi.org/10.1126/sciimmunol.aeb3809

#6649. BA’s Best Green Bean Casserole With Step-by-Step Video

This green bean casserole recipe skips the canned soup. Chris Morocco’s take on the classic Thanksgiving side pairs fresh green beans and deeply browned crimini mushrooms with a garlicky Parmesan béchamel. As for the topping, French’s fried onions are iconic for good reason, and they are staying right where they belong.

Give the mushrooms room to brown, salt the blanching water generously (like you would for cooking pasta), and taste the mushrooms and sauce before assembling. As written, you can cook the mushrooms and make the sauce at the same time. To save a pan, cook the mushrooms first, then transfer them to a plate and make the béchamel in the same pan, scraping up all the browned bits.

For the rest of the spread, turn to our classic Thanksgiving menu →

Can I make green bean casserole ahead of time?

Yes. Blanch the green beans, cook the mushrooms, and make the sauce up to 1 day ahead; cool and refrigerate them separately. Assemble and bake the day you plan to serve it, adding the fried onions during the final few minutes of baking.

We don’t recommend freezing the assembled casserole—the cream sauce can separate, and the beans turn mushy after thawing and reheating.

How do I keep the cream sauce from separating?

Don’t overreduce it. Once the béchamel is thick and bubbling, take it off the heat before whisking in the garlic and Parmesan. Boiling off too much liquid can cause the fat to separate. Stick with the recipe’s amount of Parmesan, too—extra cheese can contribute to a broken sauce.

Blanched, fresh beans are our first choice, but readers have reported success with frozen petite and French-cut beans. We haven’t tested the swap, but recommend thawing them overnight in your refrigerator and straining the excess liquid before continuing.

Can I make this green bean casserole gluten-free?

We haven’t tested a gluten-free version, but our editors suggest replacing the all-purpose flour with a gluten-free flour blend. You’ll also need to seek out gluten-free fried onions, or try our flourless Crispy Fried Shallots.

Place rack in middle of oven; preheat oven to 375°. Working in batches, cook 2 lb. fresh green beans in a large pot of boiling salted water until bright green and halfway to tenderness, about 3 minutes per batch. Drain and let cool; trim stem ends.

Heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Cook ½ lb. crimini mushrooms, sliced, without stirring, until golden brown underneath, about 2 minutes. Toss and continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until browned on both sides, about 3 minutes more. Add 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter and 2 large thyme sprigs to pan. Cook, tossing occasionally, until butter browns and mushrooms are dark brown and very tender, about 4 minutes longer. Season with kosher salt and transfer to a plate. Repeat with 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter, salt, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, ½ lb. crimini mushrooms, sliced, and 2 large thyme sprigs.

Melt remaining 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large saucepan over medium-low. Whisk in 2 Tbsp. all-purpose flour and cook, whisking occasionally, until roux is golden brown and smells mildly nutty, about 4 minutes. Whisk in 1¼ cups whole milk and 1 cup heavy cream. Increase heat and bring to a simmer, whisking often, and cook until béchamel sauce is thick and bubbling, about 5 minutes. Remove from heat and whisk in 4 garlic cloves, finely grated, and ½ cup grated Parmesan; season with salt and freshly ground pepper.

Arrange green beans and mushrooms in a 2-qt. baking dish. Pour sauce over bean mixture (it may not look like enough, but it will get saucier as it bakes). Cover tightly with foil and bake until sauce is bubbling, 25–30 minutes. Uncover and continue to bake until casserole is lightly browned on top and around the edges, 15–20 minutes longer. Top with ¾ cup French’s fried onions and continue to bake just until onions are slightly darker and fragrant, about 3 minutes. Let sit 10 minutes to set before serving.

Editor’s note: This green bean casserole recipe first appeared in November 2016 as part of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen’s definitive takes on iconic dishes. Head this way for more of our go-to Thanksgiving recipes →

#6647. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

The Defense Intelligence Agency's latest "Challenges to Security in Space" report included a declassified satellite photo of China's Shenlong, or "divine dragon," space plane, which has released at least nine mysterious payloads into low Earth orbit since 2022.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A new U.S. intelligence agency report has seemingly released the first clear photograph of China's mysterious "dragon" space plane in orbit around Earth. The surprise snap reveals that the top-secret vehicle is very similar to its American counterpart and provides new clues about its capabilities.

The image is widely believed to show China's secretive Shenlong, or "divine dragon," space plane, which has been in action for just over six years. During this time, the reusable winged spacecraft has repeatedly made headlines after deploying various unidentified objects in low Earth orbit (LEO). As a result, government officials, private companies and individual researchers have closely monitored the vehicle using tools such as ground-based radar.

Until now, the only direct images of the space plane have been blurry snaps of light reflecting off the uncrewed vehicle toward Earth's surface — offering no clear clues to its specific design, capabilities or intended purpose. China has also never publicly shared any photos of the vehicle or revealed any key information about its design.

On Monday (Oct. 26), the Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) released the latest version of its "Challenges to Security in Space" report, which assesses the various factors that pose a risk to American space assets. Deep within the 130-page document (on page 53), the authors included a previously unseen image of a "PRC [People's Republic of China] Spaceplane." The image's brief caption revealed that the photo had been taken in 2024 by a satellite belonging to the private space company Maxar Technologies, now known as Vantor.

The surprise inclusion of the photo was spotted and shared on the social platform X by journalist Andrew Jones, who specializes in China's space program and has previously shared crucial information about other ongoing missions.

The new image suggests that Shenlong looks very similar to the U.S. Space Force's X-37B space plane, which is also currently orbiting Earth.

Neither the caption nor the related section of the report made any mention of the photo being the first of its kind or explained why it was previously classified, raising questions about whether the authors realized its significance.

There is one small caveat. The report notes that China has two active space plane designs — Shenlong and Tengyun, meaning "cloud rider" — and the image's caption does not specify which design we are looking at, according to The Aviationist.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

However, there have been no confirmed launches of Tengyun to date. Existing photos of a potential prototype also hint that this vehicle's design looks markedly different from what we can see in the new photo. Therefore, most experts agree that the spacecraft in the image is most likely Shenlong.

Until now, all we really knew about Shenlong is that it operates similarly to NASA's iconic space shuttles: It gets launched into space by a rocket and circles Earth before eventually gliding down to the planet's surface, where it can then be refueled and relaunched into LEO.

It is not the world's only active space plane. The U.S. Space Force has its own, the X-37B, which has already completed seven orbital missions since its first launch in 2010 and is currently in LEO experimenting with quantum navigation. Based on the new photos, Shenlong shares many similarities with its American counterpart.

Until now, the only direct images of Shenlong were blurry snaps of light reflecting off the spacecraft back to Earth's surface.

"The Chinese spaceplane has delta wings, payload bay doors, a dark heat shield, and a rear-mounted service module with power-generating solar arrays," technology news site ArsTechnica reported. "In other words, the design of the winged ship is, to a great degree, a copy of the X-37B spaceplane flown by the U.S. Space Force."

However, the two spacecraft are not exactly the same: "The overall arrangement resembles the American vehicle, although differences in wing geometry show that the two spacecraft are not externally identical," according to specialist news site Global Defense News.

It is still unclear how large Shenlong is. The X-37B is 29 feet (8.8 meters) long and has a wingspan of 15 feet (4.5 m), according to Popular Science.

The new image also indicates that Shenlong is most likely not a military asset, Global Defense News reported, noting that "the image does not establish a weapons role."

Shenlong shares the same key design features as X-37B (right) but is not identical to its American counterpart.

However, China likely has other space-based weapons, similar to the mysterious "in-orbit" American weapons recently confirmed by U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy E. Meink.

"China has developed and will continue to advance weapons for use against satellites in orbit to disrupt, damage, and destroy other nations' space capabilities," DIA representatives wrote in a separate section of the new report. "Beijing aims to become the preeminent leader in space," they added.

Since first launching into space on an initial two-day mission in September 2020, Shenlong has completed two feature-length missions: an eight-month stint in LEO between August 2022 and May 2023, and a nine-month spaceflight between December 2023 and September 2024. (The new image was taken during the latter mission).

The space plane is currently on its fourth mission, which launched Feb. 7 on board a Long March 2F rocket from China's Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, Live Science's sister site Space.com previously reported. In total, Shenlong has racked up more than 800 days in orbit. However, it is unclear whether the same space plane was used on all four missions or if China has more than one space plane in use.

Shenlong was most recently launched into space on board a Long March 2F rocket on Feb. 7. (This image shows the same rocket during a different launch in 2011.)

So far, Shelong has released at least nine unidentified payloads around Earth. These objects are most likely small satellites, known as cubesats, but their purpose remains unclear.

The most recent object was deployed in June this year, although astronomer Jonathan McDowell, who specializes in tracking spacecraft in LEO, has since suggested that the spacecraft retrieved the object, potentially with a robotic arm, and rereleased it in late August.

The new report also mentions that the space plane "appeared to maneuver with a companion satellite" during its second mission in November 2022, coming within 330 feet (100 m) of the smaller spacecraft and potentially even capturing and re-releasing it.

This may support an existing theory that the main goal of Shenlong is to "conduct rendezvous and proximity operations" with other spacecraft, and that its payloads may be targets for it to practice flyby maneuvers in orbit.

Editor's note: This article was updated on Oct. 29 to correct a typo. A previous version of the article abbreviated the People's Republic of China as "PCR" rather than "PRC". This has been corrected.

Harry is a U.K.-based senior staff writer at Live Science. He studied marine biology at the University of Exeter before training to become a journalist. He covers a wide range of topics including space exploration, planetary science, space weather, climate change, animal behavior and paleontology. His recent work on the solar maximum won "best space submission" at the 2024 Aerospace Media Awards and was shortlisted in the "top scoop" category at the NCTJ Awards for Excellence in 2023. He also writes Live Science's weekly Earth from space series.

#6643. For Talarico and Hinojosa, Whataburger Is a Perfectly Texas Place to Celebrate

Like so many Texans on so many nights, Senator-elect James Talarico and Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa ended their evening at Whataburger.

Late Tuesday night, after Talarico flipped a Senate seat for the Democrats and Hinojosa was elected the first Democratic governor of the state in more than three decades, the two sat down at an Austin-area location of Whataburger, the iconic regional fast food chain, to clink plastic orange-and-white-striped cups.

It was a fitting setting for the pair, who played critical roles in the blue wave that swept the country in the midterm elections on Tuesday night. Talarico, who defeated scandal-plagued Republican Ken Paxton, went on the offensive against billionaires, prevailing with a positive, populist message against a party funded by Elon Musk and other ultrawealthy donors.

Hinojosa, the first Latina to be elected governor for Texas, targeted corruption and data centers in her race against Republican incumbent Greg Abbott. Both Talarico and Hinojosa will be the first Democrats in more than 30 years to serve Texas in their respective roles.

But even in the midst of a polarizing political moment for the nation, loving Whataburger is bigger than politics in Texas. Since opening its first location in Corpus Christi, Texas, in 1950, the chain, with its signature A-frame buildings, has become a social center for small towns, a place for a budget-friendly meal for families, and a crucial hangout for high schoolers figuring out where else they’ll go that night or stopping for a late-night breakfast before heading home.

Instead of popping Champagne, it’s poignant that Talarico and Hinojosa celebrated with oversize sodas. You can still get a double-burger Whatameal for under $15. These aren't the first Democrats to harness the tangy-sweet appeal of Whataburger's much-beloved Fancy Ketchup. In 2018, the campaign for senate-hopeful Beto O'Rourke shared video of him skateboarding outside a Whataburger before going inside to eat.

Today’s prices are squarely in line with the affordability politics that resonated with voters this cycle. And Talarico and Hinojosa’s Whataburger cheers was a fitting end to a campaign that wove food and politics together. While casting himself as a David against Paxton’s Goliath, Talarico absorbed attacks that claimed he was vegan. While the Senator-elect had urged residents to cut down on beef consumption, he denied the dietary restriction, countering by posting pictures of himself chowing down on barbecue.

Paxton still tried to label his opponent as “Tofu Talarico,” and Trump imagined a scenario where Talarico excuses himself to vomit after eating meat. The barbs were not-so-subtle assaults on Talarico’s manhood, the latest manifestation of the link between meat and masculinity. But there was Talarico on election night, sitting in the house of beef patties, Whatachick’n strips, and bacon-and-egg taquitos.

After a 2019 acquisition by a Chicago-based investment firm, Whataburger has faced allegations of diminishing quality and a nascent rival in Austin’s P. Terry’s Burger Stand. And still, aside from a Dairy Queen or A&W after a high school football game, there may be nowhere in Texas that feels as Texas as a Whataburger when you’re not quite ready to call it a night.

One of the defining features of Whataburger has always been its friendliness to customizing your meal—made to order. Want jalapeños and mustard on your burger, no mayo? Go right ahead, sweetie.

#6642. Soothing Rice Porridge

This is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

Remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.

I typically pack the night before a trip. So it isn't a fully “in advance” pack, but it gives me a little buffer room, so I’m not panic-packing.

My aluminum Rimowa carry-on. I just got a new travel tote by La Mama, and have been bringing that everywhere; I am obsessed with the matching pouch, too.

I typically wear a set (lately, I’ve been reaching for my Suzie Kondi velour set) with a nice, warm sweater or jacket layered on top and flats.

I bring compression socks with me on flights; my favorites are from Ricari. Also, peppermint tea.

Sweater or hoodie, always. I love my Ashlyn sweater because it’s cozy but structured—I can wear it on the plane but also on the trip itself.

I love sheet masks on vacation, especially Augustinus Bader and 111Skin face masks. I have also been really into using my Crown Affair hair towel when I shampoo my hair; I’m taking it with me when I travel.

I don't worry too much about things getting wrinkled because I feel it is inevitable. I always have an iron sent to my room when I unpack, and I try to get that sorted from the beginning so it makes life easier on the trip.

I hate to admit it, but I am such an over-packer. I try so hard not to be, though!

Bring pieces that are super versatile—I have a leather jacket that I bring everywhere. I also try to bring pieces that make me feel super comfortable. This floral robe travels with me often.

#6639. Condensed Milk Bread Rolls

Recipe by Kallee Krong-McCreery, Escondido, California

These milk bread rolls are enriched with condensed milk, which makes them fluffy and tender with a touch of sweetness.

Baking bread is one of my biggest culinary joys. It feels magical that a handful of pantry ingredients can create a supple dough, which then transforms into tender, browned bread just begging for a slathering of butter. Whether I’m making sourdough French bread or homemade dinner rolls, the process is mostly the same, but a few small ingredient changes can give a recipe a distinct identity. In these condensed milk bread rolls, that small change is a can of sweetened condensed milk.

This recipe was inspired by Brazilian milk buns (pão de leite condensado) and Portuguese sweet bread, which have sweetened condensed milk added to the dough for flavor and a sugary edge. Most of these recipes use a starter technique called tangzhong, where a cooked flour paste is kneaded into the dough to create a fluffy, cloud-like texture similar to that of Japanese milk bread. We simplified the process for our buns, skipping the starter so they come together without advanced planning.

In a small bowl, dissolve the yeast in warm water. In a large bowl, combine the milk, eggs, butter, sugar, vanilla, salt, yeast mixture and 1-1/2 cups of flour. Beat the mixture on medium speed for three minutes until it’s smooth. Stir in enough of the remaining flour to form a soft dough.

Turn the dough onto a floured surface and knead it until it’s smooth and elastic, six to eight minutes. Place the dough in a greased bowl, turning once to grease the top. Cover the bowl and let the dough rise in a warm place until it has doubled in size, about one hour.

Editor’s Tip: When kneading, start with a light dusting of flour, adding more only as needed. It’s normal for dough enriched with eggs and butter to be tacky initially (it eases as you knead and develop gluten), but adding too much flour will make the bread dry.

Punch down the dough. Turn it out onto a lightly floured surface, then divide and shape it into 12 balls. Place the dough balls in a greased 13×9-inch baking pan. Preheat the oven to 350°. Meanwhile, cover the pan with a kitchen towel and let the rolls rise in a warm place until they have almost doubled in size, 45 to 60 minutes longer.

Editor’s Tip: For evenly-sized rolls, divide the dough by weight using a kitchen scale. The best kitchen scales offer measurements in grams and ounces, so you can divvy up the dough easily no matter which system you prefer.

Bake the rolls until they’re lightly browned, 15 to 20 minutes. Cover the pan loosely with foil if the tops brown too quickly.

Since these rolls are yeast-based and require two rises, you have to make them at least a few hours ahead of time, but you can stretch that to the day before. Make the dough as directed, but cover and refrigerate them after shaping and placing them in the baking dish. The next day, let the rolls warm and rise at room temperature before baking them as directed.

You can freeze baked condensed milk bread rolls for up to three months in an airtight, freezer-proof food storage container. Thaw them in the refrigerator, then warm them in a low oven, around 300°, until they’re soft.

Dense or dry rolls are usually the result of underproofing, overbaking or adding too much flour. Proofing gives the yeast time to lift the heavy dough, weaving air into it for a light texture. If the dough doesn’t rise enough, the lack of air produces rolls with a tight, firm crumb. Use the time cues in this recipe as a guide—proofing may take longer in a chilly kitchen, or go faster on a hot day.

Overbaked rolls can be dry or hard because the extended oven time pulls out their moisture. Since ovens vary, set a timer and check them a few minutes early—even three to four extra minutes can make a big difference. They could also be dry if you knead in too much flour, or if you didn’t measure your flour correctly from the start. Extra flour will hydrate as it proofs, sucking up the liquid that would otherwise contribute to tender rolls.

You can tell yeast is active when a creamy, foamy layer forms on the water’s surface a few minutes after mixing it with warm water. It looks like frothy, milky coffee! Although you don’t always have to proof yeast depending on the type and recipe, proofing active dry yeast gives you visual confirmation that it’s viable. Sometimes the yeast can die off even before the expiration date; proofing checks for that. Once the dough is mixed, you’ll see active yeast at work as it starts to expand, rise and relax the dough.

These lightly sweetened rolls are versatile and can be served for breakfast or brunch with your favorite frittata, crispy bacon and a bowl of fruit salad, or with afternoon tea or dinner. The flavor of the condensed milk—especially as it caramelizes on the roll’s tops—would pair especially well with pork chop dinners, which often feature a sweet ingredient. I also want to try them as a twist on croissant ice cream sandwiches in place of the flaky French pastry.

This recipe doesn’t use a whole can of sweetened condensed milk, but don’t toss the rest. Put it to work in other sweetened condensed milk recipes, or try something new and shake up a Vietnamese coffee martini. Better yet, serve condensed milk rolls with the martini for a happy hour to remember.

#6638. Apple Juice Bread

A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level. The subtle, but unmistakable, undercurrent of apple sweetness struck me as a bit of a magic trick in a bread that, otherwise, to the eye and hand was just a soft white loaf.

I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal. When I asked him what he did differently to prepare it, he said he just took the same rustic bread recipe he baked elsewhere and used apple juice in place of water. I was incredulous. That was it? The same amount? The same technique? Yes and yes, he said. I was hooked. It turns out the water-to-juice switcheroo gives an added taste of fall without taking anything away from the shape and texture. It’s become an instant favorite at my house both breakfast and lunch, and I expect it will be at yours.

Take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed. You can do it!

More apple recipes here: 37 Apple Desserts That Make Us Want to Pick the Whole Orchard

Mix 4 cups (500 g) all-purpose flour, 1¾ cups apple juice, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. sugar, and one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) in a large bowl just until flour is hydrated and a very shaggy dough forms, about 1 minute. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit at room temperature 15 minutes.

Set a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough, dip your hand in water and stretch one side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat 3 more times, turning bowl 90° after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Wet your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat folding process to make 1 full fold. Re-cover and let dough sit another 30 minutes. Repeat folding process and resting one more time. By the last fold, dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Transfer dough to a generously floured surface, dust with flour, and shape into a tight ball. Dust dough with more flour. Dust a kitchen towel with flour and place inside a high-sided bowl to line. Arrange dough, seam side up, in bowl on top of towel. Tightly cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven, then set a large ovenproof Dutch oven with a lid on it; preheat oven to 400°. Place a 12" square of parchment paper on a flat surface. Cut a 2"-long slit in each corner toward the center. Very carefully, tip dough out onto center of parchment, trying your best not to deflate it or ruin its shape. (It’s easiest to place parchment on a flat plate so you can easily turn dough out of bowl.) Working very quickly and using a pair of kitchen shears lightly coated in vegetable oil, cut an X in center of bread. Remove pot from oven and very carefully lower dough into pot. Cover pot and return to oven.

Bake bread 35 minutes. Uncover pot, reduce oven temperature to 375°, and continue to bake bread until crust is deeply browned, 35–40 minutes more. Carefully tip loaf out onto a wire rack and let cool at least 1 hour before slicing.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 3 days ahead. Let cool completely; store airtight at room temperature.

#6635. This Fashion Scion’s Laid-Back Ibiza Wedding Featured Lace Dresses, Barefoot Vows, and Dancing Till Dawn

It took the world grinding to a halt for Lola Teller, 29, and Freddie Woodruff, 35, to get going. A mutual friend had set them up on a date in 2020, but with Lola studying in Edinburgh and Freddie building his catering business, Noco, in London, geography got in the way. That is, until 12 months later, when lockdown found them separated by little more than a field in Boscastle, Cornwall, where Lola’s mother, fashion photographer and stylist Venetia Scott, owns a house, and Freddie was setting up a restaurant. “He used to come and cook for us every night, and a few weeks in, my mum was like, ‘Look, why don’t you come and live with us here?’” Lola says. “She was very fond of him, and I think she liked the food, so she was pushing.” What followed was an idyllic few months spent picking mussels on the beach and taking boats out into the Celtic Sea to catch lobsters. Eventually, though, it was time for Lola to begin her career in the art world—she is now director of the agenda-setting Bernheim gallery—and the couple moved in together in leafy north-west London. This time for good.

It was in July 2025 that Lola and Freddie got engaged, while staying at her family home on Hydra, where she has spent summers since childhood. “Fred decided he wanted to go on a hike at 4 p.m. in the boiling heat, and I was like, ‘This is ridiculous, no way,’” she says. “Something must be going on.” With nerves and temperatures running high, they barely spoke on the way up, and Freddie almost lost the ring—a trio of east-to-west oval Sophie Breitmeyer diamonds—among the rocks. “We got to the top of the mountain, completely dehydrated, just as the sun was setting, when he told me to sit on a rock and got down on one knee,” she recalls. “And it was really quite beautiful.” From there, the would-be-weds jetted off to Es Cucons, a family-run hotel in northern Ibiza, where the owners, who had been welcoming Lola and her mother for years, offered to host their wedding. “They said, ‘We don’t usually do this, but how does 40 guests sound?’, and we were like, ‘...150?’” They settled on 90, returning to the hotel at Christmas, Easter, and once more the following summer to finalize the plans.

There were even more visits—10 in total—to Kensington-based bridal designer Phillipa Lepley to perfect the lace wedding dress, complete with corset, veil, and train, and designed with the input of her mom. Having a mother behind some of Vogue’s most memorable covers must have come in handy? “Throughout the process, she was making me try on these enormous poofs of dresses, which looked great but were never gonna be the one for me,” Lola says. “Often I’d be like, ‘I like this!’, and then mum would be like, ‘...No.’ She’s always right, though.”

On the day, she paired the dress with white silk platform heels from “not a nice brand,” and diamond-and-pearl drop earrings borrowed from her stepmother’s collection. She would walk down the aisle flanked by her mom and dad, Juergen Teller, though despite having two of fashion’s most directional photographers at her fingertips, she still hired traditional wedding photographers to document the occasion. “Well, you want some of the classic shots,” she explains. “Plus, they wanted to enjoy themselves.” Indeed, Lola says Teller didn’t take “a single photo” throughout the weekend.

Which began with guests gathering for welcome cocktails among the fig and almond trees of the farmhouse hotel, before Lola, Freddie, and their closest family members headed to Chiringuito Cala Xuclar for an intimate dinner of grilled fish on the beach. “I think I had an hour of sleep that night,” Lola says, “which might have been because we were drinking quite late, but also… the nerves.” The morning of the wedding began with Lola kicking Freddie out of their room, before setting off on an hour-long coastal walk with her mum and bridesmaids. Saunas and ice baths followed, as they took their time getting ready for the ceremony. Once laced into her dress, Lola made her way up the hillside to a secluded grove, where her Armani-clad groom was waiting. Flanked by her parents, she walked down the aisle to Mazzy Star’s “Fade Into You,” though her entrance didn’t go entirely to plan. “It’s such a slow song, so it was really hard to time,” she says. “My veil got caught on a stone and nearly ripped my head off, which made it quite comical.” Following behind was a giddy procession of flower girls in La Coquetta dresses, among them her three-year-old sister, all walking at their own pace. “My 12-year-old goddaughter was sending me dresses that were, like, £500 each. Nice try.”

Lola’s uncle officiated the ceremony, which included a poem written by Freddie’s mother, a group singalong to Bob Marley’s “One Love,” and Lola tossing her bouquet as the newlyweds made their way back down the aisle. “I was ready for a drink at that point,” she says. “It was time.” The couple joined their loved ones in the hotel gardens for canapés of padrón peppers, octopus skewers, croquettes, and jamón, along with speeches and photographs, before everyone was ushered into a candlelit pergola for dinner, waving their napkins in the air to The Shapeshifters’ “Lola’s Theme.”

Dinner was served family-style: lamb chops, roast potatoes, and Spanish salads, before Lola steeled herself to make a speech of her own. “I was petrified, about to burst into tears,” she says. “But after a few drinks, it was fine, and I’m so glad I did it.” The room then erupted into an impromptu rendition of John Denver’s “Take Me Home, Country Roads,” giving Lola a chance to slip away and change into a beaded Clio Peppiatt minidress.

Back at the tables, a giant slab of tiramisu was wheeled in for the newlyweds to serve to their guests, who were in no hurry to move on. “I was like, ‘Guys, they’ve literally converted the yoga tent into a dance floor.’” DJ Fiona Jane played Ibiza bangers until 12:30 a.m., before the party spilled out around the swimming pool. “They were up till seven—the sign of a good wedding,” Lola says. “Freddie and I were asleep, luckily.”

The following morning was a slow one, with guests resurfacing in the afternoon for enormous pans of poolside paella—under mercifully cloudy skies, after days spent seeking refuge from the sun beneath parasols and behind fans—as friends of the couple took turns behind the decks. Lola wore a lace beach dress by Away That Day over a white bikini, before changing into a crochet Reformation number for one final hurrah at legendary nightlife institution Pikes. Well, the last official hurrah, anyway.

A handful of guests extended their stay, dropping in on the newlyweds at Atzaró Agroturismo Hotel—a 13-hectare farm-to-fork property where the tinkling of goats’ bells drifts over from neighboring farms and chickens roam freely—for a few days of decompression before Lola returned to London for the annual art-world frenzy that is Frieze. “A lot of people say that they come back and they have loads of wedding blues, but I just didn’t; I was just so happy that everything went so perfectly,” she says. “The whole thing was surreal, just the best feeling, heaven. I’ve spent every day since looking at the photos and trying to relive the happiest memories with our favorite people.”

Dancing into dinner to “Lola’s Theme” by The Shapeshifters.

Archaeologists found several ancient weapons, intact vases and a bronze razor in the volcanic crater lake.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have recovered a well-preserved bronze sword from a volcanic lake in Italy. The 3,300-year-old weapon may have been deposited in the lake as an offering to a deity or for a high-status warrior who lived long before the rise of the Etruscans or the Romans.

The sword was found in Lake Mezzano, which is located in the crater of an ancient volcano roughly 60 miles (100 kilometers) northwest of Rome, according to a translated statement from the Superintendence of Archaeology, Fine Arts and Landscape for the Province of Viterbo and Southern Etruria. Dating to the Late Bronze Age (14th to 13th centuries B.C.), the sword has maintained its sharp edge. It is the third such sword found in Lake Mezzano in the past 50 years.

Bronze Age people erected pile dwellings or stilt houses in what is now Lake Mezzano, and archaeologists recovered parts of the submerged settlement during their recent investigations. According to the statement, researchers also found numerous intact vases, axes, arrowheads, daggers, spearheads, pins and a bronze razor.

The bronze sword dates to the Late Bronze Age and may have been a symbol of power.

The sword and the razor were found near each other, suggesting the two artifacts may have been linked to a person of high social status, such as an elite warrior. But the placement of the metal weapons in a lake may also be related to a wider Bronze Age ritual practice where hoards of jewelry and bent or ritually "killed" artifacts were tossed into bodies of water. This practice continued through the centuries into Etruscan times, when wells were ritually "closed" with artifacts and human sacrifices.

During the 13th century B.C., people in central Italy engaged in trade networks that spanned the Mediterranean. "In this context, bronze weapons were not only instruments of combat, but also symbols of prestige, identity, and power," according to the statement.

The sword and other artifacts discovered in Lake Mezzano are giving archaeologists new information about the people who flourished in prehistoric Italy long before the Romans and Etruscans. Additional research is planned in the coming years, according to the statement.

#6633. Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup

Chicken noodle soup just got way more interesting. Inspired by Egyptian bird tongue soup, this warming spice-tinged chicken broth is as comforting as it is flavorful. The real star here is the orzo. Toasted in butter until it’s deeply golden and nutty-fragrant, the pasta takes on a new personality. Unlike plain noodles, which quickly go limp in hot soup, well-toasted orzo stays al dente for longer, holding its shape and texture until you’ve doled out every bowl.

Any store-bought chicken broth, stock, or bouillon paste offers an extra boost of flavor to the base that chicken thighs and water alone can’t compete with—for an even more robust option, go for chicken bone broth.

More nourishing soup recipes this way: Curried Yellow Squash Soup; Broken Lasagna Noodle Soup With Spinach; Spicy Cod and Potato Chowder.

Season 1¼ lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs (4–5) all over with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Heat 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large pot over medium. Add 1 tsp. crushed fennel seeds, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. ground cardamom, and ¼ tsp. ground cloves and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 20 seconds. Add chicken, one 1" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth or chicken stock, and 3 cups water. Bring to a simmer over medium-high heat. Partially cover pot, reduce heat to medium-low, and simmer until an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part of a thigh registers at least 165°, 15–18 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board and let cool slightly. Reduce heat to low and cover pot. Using 2 forks, shred chicken.

Melt 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 cup orzo and cook, stirring often, until golden brown and fragrant, about 5 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper.

Scrape orzo mixture into pot with broth. Increase heat to medium and simmer broth, uncovered, until orzo is just al dente, 8–10 minutes. Remove soup from heat and add shredded chicken, 5 oz. baby kale or spinach, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice. Stir until greens are just wilted. Taste and season with more salt if needed.

#6632. Popeye’s Is Bringing Back This Side Dish for the First Time Since the ’90s

Popeyes is bringing back a nostalgic side dish on Nov. 2, and fans will have plenty to celebrate.

There are two kinds of people in this world: those who go to Popeyes for the chicken and those who will make a special visit just to eat the Cajun fries. Personally, I’m in the second camp. Granted, I have nothing against Popeyes chicken! But the Cajun fries are so deliciously seasoned and perfectly crispy that sometimes I will drive-thru and get them as a snack.

And if you’re also a fan of Popeyes’ side dishes, I have some particularly good news. The Louisiana chicken chain is reaching into its menu archives to bring back a nostalgic favorite that hasn’t been widely available since the ’90s. Let’s just say your next Popeyes order might look a little different!

Popeyes has a long history of serving up more than just fried chicken. When the chain first opened in 1976, its menu featured everything from fried clams to chicken liver. Among those early offerings was a beloved side that eventually disappeared from menus in most markets. But it’s about to make its triumphant return because Popeyes is bringing back Cajun Onion Rings!

The hand-sliced, hand-battered onion rings were slathered with Cajun seasoning. With a distinctive crispy bite, they became a fan favorite almost immediately. In fact, I have family members who constantly compare other fast-food onion ring offerings to the Popeyes version they remember from childhood. In their memories, the Popeyes onion rings were always better!

But the onion rings slowly disappeared from menus. Some locations served them until the 1990s, but by then it was mostly a thing of the past. Now, nearly three decades later, the side dish is finally making its way back.

Onion rings are officially back on the Popeyes lineup now. Availability may vary by location, but this is when you should expect to see them on menus at your local Popeyes.

Priced at $3.99, the Cajun Onion Rings are designed for sharing, although I certainly wouldn’t blame anyone for keeping the whole order to themselves. After all, crispy onion rings are pretty hard to resist. I might even order the onion rings and fries and mix ’em together.

Will you be ordering the new Cajun Onion Rings? Let us know in the comments below!

#6630. Butterball Made a Tiny Turkey That Assigns Thanksgiving Chores—And It’s Free

Turkey, stuffing and a little accountability are on the menu this year.

There’s always that one Thanksgiving guest who says, “Just tell me what to do!” while somehow managing to avoid doing anything. Well, Butterball has a tiny turkey for that.

On Monday, Nov. 2, the turkey brand took to Instagram to introduce the Butterball Buddy, a tiny electronic taskmaster that hands out Thanksgiving chores so the host doesn’t have to. It looks like something straight out of the ’90s, and the best part? It won’t cost you a dime.

As silly as a chore-assigning turkey sounds, the company might be onto something. Its 2026 Togetherness Report found that 85% of Thanksgiving hosts would prefer guests to offer to help, but only 38% ask. Nearly half say the final cleanup is where they could use an extra hand.

Once everyone arrives, guests pass the Buddy around like a hot potato. When it chimes and vibrates, whoever’s holding it gets a task, whether that’s setting the table before dinner or tackling the dishes afterward. Finish the job, pass it along, and it’s the next lucky helper’s turn. Think Tamagotchi, except instead of keeping a digital pet alive, you’re keeping the kitchen from turning into a disaster area.

Set an alarm. The first batch dropped Nov. 2, and two more are coming at 1 p.m. ET on Monday, Nov. 9, and Monday, Nov. 16, at ButterballBuddy.com. Quantities are limited, so the early birds get the turkey. The giveaway is open to legal U.S. residents ages 18 and older, and no purchase is necessary.

The Buddies may be in short supply, but Butterball’s cooking advice isn’t. Its Turkey Talk-Line is celebrating its 45th anniversary this year, with more than 50 experts answering questions about everything from thawing to checking for doneness through Dec. 24. You can call 1-800-BUTTERBALL, text 844-877-3456 or chat live at Butterball.com. The hotline’s contact information is printed on the back of every Buddy, too.

#6629. The World's 50 Best Restaurants, According to ‘The 50’ Best List

Asador Etxebarri from the Spanish Basque Country won the title of world's best restaurant Wednesday night when The 50, the organization formerly known as 50 Best, announced its annual ranking during a ceremony in Lima, Peru. It was the first such event for The 50 in South America.

Situated between Bilbao and San Sebastián, Etxebarri claims some of the world's most famous chefs as major fans of Bittor Arginzoniz, who matches the characteristics of the wood in the grill with the plants and proteins sizzling over the flames. It was No. 2 on The 50 in 2025 and maintains one Michelin star. Tasting menus are around $337.

Wednesday was also a big night for Atomix in New York, which came in at No. 11 and was named Best Restaurant in North America. Junghyun Park took home the Chef's Choice Award.

A spot on The 50 is among the highest honors a restaurant can receive. (Disclosure: Bon Appétit editor in chief Jamila Robinson is a 50 Best Academy Chair.) The list favors some of the most expensive, elaborate cooking in the fine-dining world. It often rewards tasting menus that employ molecular gastronomy, but also celebrates the simple elegance of a Spanish grill, the sourcing mission of an Argentine steakhouse, or the laidback cool of Parisian neo-bistro.

This year’s ceremony ran into controversy earlier in the year when it was announced that it would be hosted in Abu Dhabi, which has faced criticism for human rights violations. In June, it was announced that the ceremony would instead be hosted in Peru, home to Maido, the Lima restaurant that won No. 1 last year. Maido is not eligible for this year’s list. After winning the top spot, it moves to the organization’s Best of the Best list alongside other past number ones like Barcelona’s Disfrutar and New York’s Eleven Madison Park.

Quintonil landed at No. 4. The two-Michelin starred restaurant in Mexico City led by Jorge Vallejo and Alejandra Flores, serves dishes that revolve around local, pre-Hispanic ingredients, which come together in energized and unexpected ways throughout its multi-course prix-fixe menu. A November menu listed on its website was priced around $327 per person for a meal that included lobster in a pipián verde with makrut lime, and an heirloom white corn tamal made with ayocote beans and young corn cream.

At Alchemist in Copenhagen (No. 3), chef Rasmus Munk oversees a meal that skews sci-fi with dishes that mimic brains and eyeballs and a show that advertises “up to 50 impressions,” both edible and “purely experiential.” It holds two Michelin stars and was ranked fifth on The 50 last year.

Gaggan in Bangkok (No. 2) claimed the title of Asia's Best Restaurant behind the creative, genre-bending Indian cooking of Gaggan Anand.

Critics of the World’s 50 Best have raised questions around its voting practices, which do not demand that voters pay for their own meals. The organization, for its part, explains that the list is voted on by more than 1,100 voters across 28 regions, a quarter of whom are new each year. The voting body is made up of equal parts chefs and restaurateurs, food writers, and “well-travelled gourmets,” as the The 50 website puts it. Aside from the Academy Chairs, voters must remain anonymous.

There is no set criteria for what makes a restaurant the best, and “every style of restaurant in the world is eligible,” though the list skews completely towards high-end dining even as other best-of links have begun to include street food venues, for instance.

Ana Ros, the chef at three Michelin-starred Hisa Franko in Slovenia, published a statement on Instagram last month explaining why she would not attend the ceremony in Lima. “Success within the ranking has come to depend increasingly on visibility within the system,” she wrote. “…When visibility becomes the currency, the ability to promote a restaurant in this system risks becoming as important as the work happening inside it.”

Ros, who won the award for best female chef from The 50 in 2017, told Bon Appétit that restaurants and tourism boards “more or less” know who the anonymous voters are, and they often have to make decisions about whether to pay for travel, meals, and other entertainment to try and boost their standing.

“With more rules and a little bit more control, this list can really shine again,” she said in an interview.

Hisa Franko was No. 60 on the ranking of 51-100 this year. It was 69th last year and No. 48 in 2024.

Ros said seeing her restaurant at any place on the list was “a fantastic result” and she would be wishing everyone all the best at the ceremony.

#6628. Brûléed Kheer (Rice Pudding) With Mango Sorbet

This creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

Note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, quickly empty the contents into a new pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

To a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

Scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.

Colorectal cancer in young people shows genetic and structural differences that may make it more aggressive and treatment-resistant than the cancer tends to be in older people.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Colorectal cancer rates have been rising in people under 50 since the mid-1990s. These early-onset cancers tend to be more aggressive and resistant to treatment than cancers in older adults — and now, scientists may be learning why.

A new study published Thursday (Oct. 29) in the journal Nature Medicine compared colorectal tumors from people between 29 and over 90 years old, and it revealed key differences between young and old patients.

The new findings might, in turn, help scientists uncover new ways to fight colorectal cancer in young people, said study co-author Ana Anderson, a professor of neurology at Harvard Medical School and a core faculty member of the Gene Lay Institute of Immunology and Inflammation at Brigham and Women's Hospital.

"I believe that our study is essentially a turning point now in the field," Anderson told Live Science. "Because up until now, we've had more questions than answers."

Many questions surround early-onset colorectal cancer, as the disease is rising in people under 50 even as it falls in older populations. It's now the leading cause of cancer death in the U.S. for people under 50, and its numbers are even on the rise among children and adolescents.

Beyond questions about what's driving this uptick in cases, another mystery has been why this disease is so deadly in young people.

"The clinical data suggests that the disease in the younger patients is more aggressive overall," Anderson said. "The patients, being very healthy otherwise, do not do well with treatment."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The reason why colorectal cancer is often aggressive in younger patients hasn't been clear.

To investigate that mystery, Anderson collaborated with Dr. Kimmie Ng, an oncologist at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, and Dr. Ramnik Xavier, a gastroenterologist at the Broad Institute and Mass General Brigham. They used a method of analyzing RNA in cells that allowed them to work with frozen and banked tumor tissue. RNA, a cousin of DNA, reflects the genes that are active in cells. In all, the team analyzed 189 tumors: 54 from patients under 50 and 135 from patients over 50.

With that many samples, the researchers could look at gradual differences tied to each age group, instead of just comparing tumors between the younger and older groups overall. That enabled them to pinpoint subtle differences, Anderson said.

For starters, younger people had a higher proportion of connective tissue cells in their tumors than they did of malignant cancer cells. That pattern was flipped in patients of older ages. Having a smaller proportion of malignant cells might sound good, but connective tissue in tumors can secrete compounds that suppress the immune system, Anderson said. That helps protect the tumor from immune cells that might otherwise target its cells for destruction.

These connective tissue cells can also physically block chemotherapy drugs from getting to the cancerous cells. This could be one reason younger patients' cancers resist treatment, the researchers suggested.

Based on patterns of gene activity in the tumors, the researchers suspect that younger patients' cancer cells also show distinct activity related to cell-to-cell communication. That may help the cells migrate through the body more easily than cancer cells in older patients do. In other cancers, this kind of gene activity has been linked to more aggressive tumors and a greater chance that the disease will spread, or metastasize, Anderson said.

The study's results also turned up an intriguing mystery: the presence of lots of long noncoding RNA. These strands of RNA contain more than 200 building blocks, called nucleotides, that don't provide instructions for building proteins. Coding RNA, in contrast, is ferried to protein-building factories in cells to be used as blueprints.

Scientists don't know what much of this long noncoding RNA does in the body, nor do they understand what it is doing in the tumors specifically. However, they hope to find out.

Anderson and her team are already working on manipulating the RNA they found inside cancer cells in petri dishes. In time, this line of research could supply another piece of the puzzle, helping scientists understand why colorectal cancer is so aggressive in young people.

"It's a new avenue for research into this disease that we previously had no idea about," Anderson said.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice

Porter, C.B.M., et al. (2026) Insights into early-onset colorectal cancer from a single-nucleus RNA-seq atlas of colorectal cancer across the age continuum. Nature Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-026-04721-y

Stephanie Pappas is a contributing writer for Live Science, covering topics ranging from geoscience to archaeology to the human brain and behavior. She was previously a senior writer for Live Science but is now a freelancer based in Denver, Colorado, and regularly contributes to Scientific American and The Monitor, the monthly magazine of the American Psychological Association. Stephanie received a bachelor's degree in psychology from the University of South Carolina and a graduate certificate in science communication from the University of California, Santa Cruz.

#6626. Ditch Your Fleet of Coffeemakers—The Chefman Coffee Station Pro Handles Everything

Can't decide between a drip coffee maker, Nespresso, Keurig or an espresso machine? The Chefman Coffee Station Pro does all four—and takes up very little room.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

As Kevin Malone famously said in Season 8, Episode 2 of The Office, “Why waste time say lot word when few word do trick?” In my opinion, the same concept should apply to countertop appliances. After ditching my microwave, countertop oven, air fryer and toaster for the all-encompassing Panasonic HomeChef, I began to wonder what else I could condense into a singular appliance.

After musing over my fleet of five(!!!) coffeemakers consisting of Keurig and Nespresso machines, an automatic espresso maker, a manual espresso maker and a classic drip coffeemaker, I realized that it was time to address the barista elephant in the room. I had to reclaim my coffee bar counter space—but how? The answer, it turns out, is the Chefman Coffee Station Pro.

Here’s how I tested it over several months and why it’s become my go-to coffee machine.

Can't decide on a brew method? The Chefman Coffee Station Pro tackles them all. Yes, really.

In the age of the all-in-one appliance, maximizing countertop space just makes sense. In small kitchens especially, cramming half a dozen different-yet-similar appliances into limited space feels like such a waste. And sure, you don’t need both a blender and a food processor, but it’s nice to have the choice between the two. That’s why combo machines like the Ninja CrushBoss came out and started changing the game. That’s also the idea behind the Chefman Coffee Station Pro.

Unlike other x-in-one machines that incorporate a couple of different brewing methods (looking at you, Keurig K-Duo), the Chefman Coffee Station Pro combines 10 different functionalities into one machine. Craving a quick single cup? You can use it with both K-cups and Nespresso pods. Need to fill up a full carafe for a party? It does that, too. But what if you want to leisurely enjoy an iced latte or a shot of espresso on the weekend? Well, that’s also an option with the built-in manual espresso machine and automatic milk frother.

In terms of functionality, the Chefman Coffee Station Pro offers espresso, cappuccino, latte, single-serve coffee, 12-cup carafe, cold brew, cold-pressed espresso, coffee over ice, hot milk and cold foam. To try it out, I packed up all my other coffee makers and made it my primary coffee machine for two months.

You’d probably expect a machine with so many capabilities to be enormous, heavy, complicated, unwieldily. Not so with the Coffee Station Pro. It’s so simple to set up and use, I didn’t even need to read through the provided booklet before I was whipping up drinks. It also takes up barely more space than a dedicated espresso machine.

Right off the bat, I brewed a pot of drip coffee. First, I’m super impressed with the way the machine can read what I’m brewing based on the basket insert I choose. Pop in the drip basket, and it’s prompting me to choose the number of cups. Swap it out with the K-Cup pod holder, and it’s now asking how many ounces I’d like. It’s truly like magic!

Then, there’s the customization. First, pick between a single cup or a whole carafe. Then, choose to enjoy your coffee either hot or over ice. You also get the option of brewing a cup or a whole pot of cold brew for summertime get-togethers. There’s even a delay brew function, which makes it easy to prep your poison of choice the night before.

As I mentioned, the machine changes its touchscreen prompts based on which brew basket you choose. When you pop in a K-cup, you’re given the option of having it hot or over ice. There’s also a choice of 4-, 6-, 8-, 10- and 12-ounce cups. Then, you can adjust the strength and temperature, with three different settings for each. Finally, there’s a small flip-down platform to rest your cup on so that it doesn’t splash everywhere as it brews.

Want to use a Nespresso capsule instead? A pod insert pops into the K-cup adapter. Again, the machine will intuit this automatically and adjust accordingly. Overall, this aspect of the machine is incredibly intuitive. Plus, you can save specific settings as one of three “favorites,” if you want to speed things up with one-touch operation.

As for espressos, this thing does work. It boasts a 20-bar pressure system that brews espressos topped in a beautiful, silky crema. Pick from a single or double shot, or opt for a cappuccino or latte, both with a choice of single or double. If you choose a milk-based drink, ensure the milk reservoir is filled and angle the metal wand into your cup—the machine does the rest.

If you’re familiar with a standard manual espresso machine, you already know how to operate the portafilter. If not, no worries—there are helpful videos from Chefman to guide you through the process. You can also opt for hot milk, or warm or cold foam on its own by choosing the “froth” setting if you want to add any of those to your cup of regular coffee.

On the top of the machine next to the brew basket is an area with accessory storage for the portafilter baskets, Nespresso adapter and combination scoop/tamper. On the side of the coffee station is a place to stow the portafilter. While there’s no built-in storage for the brew basket, K-cup basket and carafe when they’re not in use, I do love that the smaller accessories have a dedicated space so they won’t be misplaced.

In terms of cleaning, this might be one of the easier machines I’ve ever used. All of the inserts simply rinse clean. But the part I really love is the milk frother. Instead of nooks and crannies that collect smells and residue, the entire thing comes apart into several pieces, so you can thoroughly rinse and wash every single part that touches milk. Win!

Chefman isn’t the only brand to claim that they’ve created an “all-in-one” solution for flexible baristas. In our research, we also found three other similar machines: The De’Longhi All-in-One, the Ninja Prestige Dual Brew Coffee Maker and, of course, the classic  Keurig K-Duo.

The only issue? We couldn’t find a single other appliance that offered K-Cup compatibility and Nespresso pod capability and a carafe and a manual espresso machine and automated milk frothing/latte settings. All of the options above offer at least two functions. Maybe four. But not all five. That crown belongs to the Chefman Coffee Station Pro alone.

Hopefully, we see more options pop up in the near future. But for now, the Chefman Coffee Station Pro is in its own category of coffee maker.

In my home, I used to have five different coffeemakers, including a Keurig, a Nespresso, an automatic espresso machine, a manual espresso maker and a classic drip coffeemaker. In fact, there were so many appliances that they began spilling into my dining room after I ran out of space on my dedicated coffee bar. After converting to the Chefman Coffee Station Pro, I’ve pared that number down to just one. One!

The only changes I’d make after using this machine since August 2026 are minor gripes. I do wish that there was a built-in coffee grinder, since having a separate bean grinder means having yet another appliance. And while I appreciate that there is a small storage cavity for tinier accessories, I don’t love having to find a place in my cupboard for the carafe and basket inserts when I’m not using them.

But honestly? Even with these small annoyances, I wouldn’t even knock off a full star on my final rating. The size, ease of use and cleanliness of the machine make it more than worth it—especially for flexible home baristas like me.

Condense five coffeemakers into just one with this ingenious appliance.

Want to clear up your counter space and join me in the future? You can snag this new appliance on the Chefman website or on Amazon. At $400, the Coffee Station Pro is absolutely an investment. And for some folks who won’t use all the different settings, it may not be worth the cost. But for coffee lovers who want to brew based on vibes (or who already have a long lineup of machines like I used to), the price point feels totally fair. After all, you’re getting five different machines in one!

The easier question is what can’t it make? It’s capable of espresso, single-serve coffee, a 12-cup carafe, cold brew and coffee over ice. While it’s not programmable to make specific drinks such as a cafe crema or Americano like some automatic espresso machines, the manual espresso component and automatic milk frother still offers extreme flexibility for budding baristas.

As Taste of Home’s shopping editor, Emily has covered everything from Pioneer Woman kitchen launches to finding the best pizza ovens. She also has four years of experience in shopping editor roles at Reader’s Digest, Taste of Home and Family Handyman. Her specialties lie in food and drink categories, as well as appliance testing and deal sourcing. Before writing this piece, we conducted three hours of research and tested the appliance for two months.

#6625. Why Martine Rose is So Right for Balenciaga

It’s major news that Martine Rose has been announced as Creative Director title at Balenciaga. Despite the fact that internet speculation over her appointment as successor to Pierpaolo Piccioli has run rife in the past weeks, long experience tells that, much like election results, it’s never real until it’s official.

The joy and relief felt by Rose’s very long-term fans might well be compared to the sensation Democrat-leaning voters are feeling at the midterm results in the US. She’s a designer’s designer, a champion of subcultures and outsiders, a woman whose huge influence as a shaper and shifter of fashion couldn’t be be more respected—and yet who’s never been tapped for a position at the top of luxury fashion since she started out as an independent London designer in 2002. This has nothing to do with the out-going designer at Balenciaga. It’s the fact that the furious wait and the endless hopes held out for Rose’s talent to be recognized and empowered in the constellation of luxury fashion has gone on far, far too long.

But now that it’s Balenciaga that finally came calling it couldn’t feel more right—not least because the Jamaican-British 46-year-old heroine of elevated street-style arrives as no stranger. It was back in 2015 that Demna, a long-distance fan who’d discovered her first presentations on the internet, hired Rose as a consultant when he was inaugurating the first Balenciaga menswear collections. I recognized her there from her low-key London shows, smilingly egging Demna on in her quiet way behind the scenes while I was working on a Vogue feature about him.

They conspired eye-to-eye on what Rose later described to me as her “observational” way of designing: looking at real life and exaggerating or twisting garments so that the familiar becomes desirable and slyly coded all over again.

At the time, Demna’s Balenciaga menswear became a massive (pun intended) hit, with its XXXL tailoring, gigantic parkas, humungous trainers, and various satirizations of unraveling corporate manhood, untucked shirts, desperate neckties, and all. As this formed the basis of the Balenciaga brand attraction that drew young shoppers around the world, it makes sense that Rose could be the woman with the insight and instincts to drive it forward now.

“I really love clothes. I’m so interested in how people wear them, and their cultural meaning,” she once told me, after one of the typically sporadic, hyper-local shows she’s been drawing audiences to in London with her own Martine Rose brand. Famed for showing on a neighborhood square in Chalk Farm for spring 2019 (Virgil Abloh came to applaud), at her daughter’s junior school in fall 2020, and most recently in a market stall scenario she’d set up in a disused Job Centre, Rose’s ethos is a unique hybrid of joyful community warmth and hardcore subversion. One of the jacquards she had woven into some of her ‘School’ collection read “Tottenham, Croydon, Clapham Junction, Tooting”—all the London boroughs she and her extended family have lived in since she was growing up in the 1980s and 1990s.

“Honoring the Jamaican family I come from” is a point of pride in her work, not to mention the encyclopedic enjoyment she takes in all the subcultures and club cultures she and her elder siblings grew up around, everything from football casuals to rave, reggae, queer culture, underground fetish, and references to club flyers or Jamaican home furnishings.

Abetted by Tamara Rothstein, her stylist friend with whom she first set up a short-lived t-shirt line, LMNOP, in 2002, Rose’s tweaks in proportions have proved so prophetic that, looking back, some of her early collections, thought to be weird at the time, now look nearly regular. In fall 2019 she remembered the reaction to her first oversized clothes. “It’s so funny,” she laughed.” When I first did this shape in spring 2013, people were like, ‘ugh, what is that’?” Simply, it became what all of us wore, and largely still do, thanks to her.

Some may ask if Rose can do womenswear and accessories. “I love playing with gender lines. I find it very sexy—a woman in men’s clothes, a man in women’s clothes,” she once told me. Her multi-generational family of favorite models bears this out. Models in Rose’s own age group have lately been commanding a powerful kind of runway sisterhood. Balenciaga—no, the whole of fashion—could definitely benefit from seeing more of that right now.

As for accessories? One only need to look shoe-ward to see what Rose has already done: her spring-heeled Nike Shox MR4 trainers are widely popular and there’s no discounting the influence of her box-toed loafers and sharp elongated pumps. All the above is a bit of an outline of the experience and joie de vivre Martine Rose brings to the party. In a time when fashion has gone a bit tame and quiet, it’s exciting to think what a woman like this will do with a free rein and such a generous feeling for human self-expression.
